elizabeth-david.name: Elizabeth David
elizabeth-david.summary: British cookery writer who revitalised home cooking in mid-20th-century Britain with books on Mediterranean and other European cuisines, beginning in 1950.

a-book-of-mediterranean-food.name: A Book of Mediterranean Food
a-book-of-mediterranean-food.summary: Elizabeth David's influential 1950 cookbook, drawn from her time in France, Italy and Greece, that reintroduced fresh Mediterranean ingredients to postwar English cooking.

michelin-guide.name: Michelin Guide
michelin-guide.summary: Restaurant and hotel guide published by the French tyre company Michelin since 1900, awarding up to three stars to top restaurants via anonymous inspectors.

chicken-tikka-masala.name: Chicken tikka masala
chicken-tikka-masala.summary: A curry of roasted marinated chicken in a spiced creamy sauce, likely invented in Glasgow, and now one of Britain's most popular dishes.

veeraswamy.name: Veeraswamy
veeraswamy.summary: An Indian restaurant in London opened in 1926, which by 2006 was the oldest Indian restaurant in the United Kingdom and won a Michelin star in 2016.

sylhet.name: Sylhet
sylhet.summary: A city in northeastern Bangladesh on the Surma River, known for tea plantations and historically ruled by the Mughals, British and Nawabs of Bengal.

balti-food.name: Balti
balti-food.summary: A curry cooked quickly over high heat in a pressed-steel wok, using vegetable oil, garlic, onions and spices like turmeric and garam masala; developed in Birmingham, England in the 1970s.

sylhetis.name: Sylhetis
sylhetis.summary: An Indo-Aryan ethnic group from the Sylhet region of Bangladesh and nearby India, with large diaspora communities in Britain, the US and Canada.

bombay-brasserie.name: Bombay Brasserie
bombay-brasserie.summary: An Indian restaurant that opened in Kensington, London, in 1982, credited as a pioneer in serving the kind of food actually eaten in India.

tamarind-restaurant.name: Tamarind
tamarind-restaurant.summary: Indian restaurant in Mayfair, London, opened in 1995, which became one of the first Indian restaurants in London to win a Michelin star, in 2001.

the-fat-duck.name: The Fat Duck
the-fat-duck.summary: Fine dining restaurant in Bray, Berkshire, owned by chef Heston Blumenthal, known for precision, innovation and multi-sensory dishes; named the world's best restaurant in 2005.

bray-berkshire.name: Bray, Berkshire
bray-berkshire.summary: A village on the River Thames in Berkshire, home to two of the UK's nine three-Michelin-starred restaurants.

the-waterside-inn.name: The Waterside Inn
the-waterside-inn.summary: A three-Michelin-star restaurant in Bray, Berkshire, founded by brothers Michel and Albert Roux and now run by Michel's son Alain; in 2010 it became the first restaurant outside France to hold three stars for 25 years.

confit-byaldi.name: Confit byaldi
confit-byaldi.summary: A variation on traditional French ratatouille created by chef Michel Guérard, later used to reinterpret the rustic dish for haute cuisine.

auguste-escoffier.name: Auguste Escoffier
auguste-escoffier.summary: French chef (1846–1935) who modernised French cooking, codified the five mother sauces, and created the kitchen brigade system still used today.

allemande-sauce.name: Sauce allemande
allemande-sauce.summary: French mother sauce of egg-and-cream-thickened veal, chicken or shellfish velouté, renamed 'sauce parisienne' during World War I because of its German name.

betty-blue.name: Betty Blue
betty-blue.summary: 1986 French erotic psychological drama film directed by Jean-Jacques Beineix, based on Philippe Djian's 1985 novel, nominated for the Academy Award for Best Foreign Language Film.

blood-swept-lands-and-seas-of-red.name: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red
blood-swept-lands-and-seas-of-red.summary: A 2014 public art installation in the Tower of London's moat marking World War I's centenary, with 888,246 ceramic poppies each representing one British or Colonial serviceman killed.
blood-swept-lands-and-seas-of-red.source_title: Blood Swept Lands and Seas of Red

david-cameron.name: David Cameron
david-cameron.summary: A British politician who served as Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 2010 to 2016 and later as Foreign Secretary from 2023 to 2024.

historic-royal-palaces.name: Historic Royal Palaces
historic-royal-palaces.summary: An independent charity that has managed the UK's unoccupied royal palaces, including the Tower of London and Hampton Court Palace, since 1989.

paul-cummins.name: Paul Cummins
paul-cummins.summary: English artist, born 1977 in Chesterfield, who creates landscape installations using ceramic flowers, known for the Tower of London poppy installation.

pierre-restany.name: Pierre Restany
pierre-restany.summary: French art critic and cultural philosopher (1930–2003) who first met Yves Klein in 1955 and maintained a strong tie with him.

yves-klein.name: Yves Klein
yves-klein.summary: French artist (1928–1962), a leading figure in the Nouveau réalisme movement and pioneer of performance art who developed International Klein Blue.

nouveau-r-alisme.name: New Realism
nouveau-r-alisme.summary: An art movement founded in 1960 by critic Pierre Restany and artist Yves Klein, seeking to bring life and art closer together and often compared to Pop Art.

stockport-war-memorial-art-gallery.name: Stockport War Memorial Art Gallery
stockport-war-memorial-art-gallery.summary: A Grade II* listed building in Stockport, England, built in 1925 as the town's main memorial to those who died in the First World War, combining a memorial hall with art exhibition galleries.

greek-revival-architecture.name: Greek Revival architecture
greek-revival-architecture.summary: An architectural style reviving forms of ancient Greek temples, flourishing in the late 18th and early 19th centuries across northern Europe, the United States and newly independent Greece.

prince-henry-duke-of-gloucester.name: Prince Henry, Duke of Gloucester
prince-henry-duke-of-gloucester.summary: Third son of King George V and a member of the British royal family, who served as Australia's governor-general from 1945 to 1947, the only prince to hold that post.

marcel-duchamp.name: Marcel Duchamp
marcel-duchamp.summary: French American artist (1887-1968) who played a key role in developing the avant-garde and became known for anti-art, notably his 1917 urinal piece, Fountain.

francis-picabia.name: Francis Picabia
francis-picabia.summary: French avant-garde painter, writer and typographist (1879–1953) closely tied to Dada, whose shape-shifting style moved through Impressionism, Cubism and later Surrealism.

dada.name: Dada
dada.summary: An international art movement launched in Zürich during World War I, rejecting conventional ideas about art and society; it later influenced Surrealism, pop art and other movements.

readymades-of-marcel-duchamp.name: Readymade
readymades-of-marcel-duchamp.summary: An ordinary manufactured object chosen, modified and presented by an artist as a work of art, a concept pioneered by Marcel Duchamp from 1914 as an alternative to purely visual art.

tom-piper.name: Tom Piper
tom-piper.summary: British theatre designer (born 1964), an associate designer with the Royal Shakespeare Company since 2004, known for collaborating with director Michael Boyd.

yeomen-warders.name: Yeomen Warders
yeomen-warders.summary: Ceremonial guardians of the Tower of London, popularly called Beefeaters, who watch over prisoners and the crown jewels and have given tours since Victorian times; all are retired warrant officers with 22+ years' service.

niki-de-saint-phalle.name: Niki de Saint Phalle
niki-de-saint-phalle.summary: French American sculptor, painter and author (1930–2002), one of few female monumental sculptors, known for her colorful "Nanas" figures and the Tarot Garden.

arman.name: Arman
arman.summary: French and American artist (1928–2005) known for his Accumulations and works made by destroying and recomposing everyday objects.

c-sar-baldaccini.name: César Baldaccini
c-sar-baldaccini.summary: French sculptor (1921–1998), born Cesare Baldaccini and known as César; a leading figure of the Nouveau réalisme movement, famous for compressed car and metal sculptures and foam 'expansions.'

daniel-spoerri.name: Daniel Spoerri
daniel-spoerri.summary: Romanian-born Swiss artist and writer (1930–2024) of the Pop art movement, known for 'snare-pictures' that fix everyday objects like meal remains onto boards.

st-magnus-cathedral.name: St Magnus Cathedral
st-magnus-cathedral.summary: The oldest cathedral in Scotland, in Kirkwall, Orkney, built from 1137 in Romanesque style while Orkney was ruled by Norse earls under the Kingdom of Norway.

kirkwall.name: Kirkwall
kirkwall.summary: A port town and historic royal burgh in Orkney, Scotland's largest town in that archipelago, home to St Magnus Cathedral and first mentioned in the Orkneyinga saga.

orkney.name: Orkney
orkney.summary: An archipelago off northern Scotland with about 70 islands, inhabited for at least 10,000 years and once part of the Kingdom of Norway before joining Scotland in 1472.

ben-vautier.name: Ben Vautier
ben-vautier.summary: A French visual artist (1935-2024) known mononymously as Ben, and a leading figure of the Fluxus art movement.

fluxus.name: Fluxus
fluxus.summary: An international art movement of the 1960s and 70s, inspired by John Cage, whose artists favored chance-based performance over finished works and helped pioneer intermedia, conceptual art and video art.

george-maciunas.name: George Maciunas
george-maciunas.summary: Lithuanian American artist and organizer (1931–1978) who founded and coordinated Fluxus, an international group known for a do-it-yourself, anti-market art aesthetic.

adolf-hitler.name: Adolf Hitler
adolf-hitler.summary: Austrian-born German dictator who led Nazi Germany from 1933 until his suicide in 1945, launching the Second World War and directing the Holocaust.

battle-of-britain.name: Battle of Britain
battle-of-britain.summary: A World War II air campaign from July to October 1940 in which the Royal Air Force and Fleet Air Arm defended Britain against Germany's Luftwaffe, the first major campaign fought entirely by air forces.

the-blitz.name: The Blitz
the-blitz.summary: An eight-month bombing campaign by Nazi Germany and Fascist Italy against Britain, from September 1940 to May 1941, targeting London and other cities.

battle-of-the-atlantic.name: Battle of the Atlantic
battle-of-the-atlantic.summary: The longest continuous military campaign of World War II, running from 1939 to 1945, in which German U-boats and warships fought Allied navies for control of Atlantic shipping.

cod-wars.name: Cod Wars
cod-wars.summary: A series of 20th-century confrontations between Iceland and the United Kingdom over North Atlantic fishing rights, each ending in an Icelandic victory.

icelandic-coast-guard.name: Icelandic Coast Guard
icelandic-coast-guard.summary: Iceland's defence service, responsible for search and rescue, maritime security, national defense and law enforcement, based mainly in Reykjavík.

neville-chamberlain.name: Neville Chamberlain
neville-chamberlain.summary: British Prime Minister from 1937 to 1940, known for the policy of appeasement and the 1938 Munich Agreement, who led Britain through the first eight months of the Second World War before resigning in 1940.

winston-churchill.name: Winston Churchill
winston-churchill.summary: British statesman and Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1940 to 1945 and 1951 to 1955, who led Britain through the Second World War.

norwegian-campaign.name: Norwegian campaign
norwegian-campaign.summary: The 1940 struggle for Norway during World War II, in which Allied forces resisted the German invasion before withdrawing, leading to full German occupation.

american-expeditionary-forces.name: American Expeditionary Forces
american-expeditionary-forces.summary: The US military force sent to the Western Front in World War I, established in 1917 under General John J. Pershing.

scapa-flow.name: Scapa Flow
scapa-flow.summary: Sheltered body of water in Scotland's Orkney Islands, used by Vikings and as the UK's main naval base in both World Wars; site of the scuttled German fleet after World War I.

grand-fleet.name: Grand Fleet
grand-fleet.summary: The Royal Navy's main battle fleet during the First World War, established in 1914 and based at Scapa Flow in Scotland's Orkney Islands.

althing.name: Althing
althing.summary: Iceland's national legislature, founded in 930 at Þingvellir and considered the oldest legislature in the world.

agatha-christie.name: Agatha Christie
agatha-christie.summary: An English author (1890–1976) of 66 detective novels, best known for creating Hercule Poirot and Miss Marple; the best-selling novelist of all time.

william-shakespeare.name: William Shakespeare
william-shakespeare.summary: English playwright, poet and actor (c. 1564–1616), widely regarded as the greatest writer in the English language, known for about 39 plays and 154 sonnets.

t-s-eliot.name: T. S. Eliot
t-s-eliot.summary: A modernist poet, essayist and playwright (1888–1965) awarded the 1948 Nobel Prize in Literature, known for works including The Waste Land and for reshaping English-language poetry.

the-waste-land.name: The Waste Land
the-waste-land.summary: T. S. Eliot's 434-line poem, published in 1922, widely regarded as one of the most important English-language poems of the 20th century, known for shifting narrators and voices without a single storyline.

sylvia-beach.name: Sylvia Beach
sylvia-beach.summary: An American-born bookseller in Paris, 1887 to 1962, who ran the Shakespeare and Company bookshop and published James Joyce's Ulysses in 1922.

james-joyce.name: James Joyce
james-joyce.summary: Irish modernist novelist (1882–1941) best known for Ulysses (1922), also author of Dubliners and A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man.

ulysses-novel.name: Ulysses
ulysses-novel.summary: Modernist novel by Irish writer James Joyce, published in Paris in 1922, following three Dubliners over a single day in 1904; considered one of the most important works of modernist literature.

olympia-press.name: Olympia Press
olympia-press.summary: Paris-based publisher launched in 1953 that issued sexually explicit and avant-garde works banned elsewhere, including the first printed edition of Nabokov's Lolita.

naked-lunch.name: Naked Lunch
naked-lunch.summary: A 1959 antinovel by William S. Burroughs, told as non-chronological 'routines' following an opioid addict, controversial for its depictions of drugs and body horror.

doris-lessing.name: Doris Lessing
doris-lessing.summary: British novelist (1919–2013) who won the 2007 Nobel Prize in Literature at 87, the oldest laureate ever; her novels include The Grass Is Singing and The Golden Notebook.

southern-rhodesia.name: Southern Rhodesia
southern-rhodesia.summary: A self-governing British colony in what is now Zimbabwe, run from 1888 by Cecil Rhodes's British South Africa Company and later by a white-minority settler government with discriminatory laws.

the-grass-is-singing.name: The Grass Is Singing
the-grass-is-singing.summary: 1950 debut novel by British author Doris Lessing, set in 1940s Southern Rhodesia, following a woman's hasty marriage, mental decline and murder amid colonial racial politics.

v-s-naipaul.name: V. S. Naipaul
v-s-naipaul.summary: A Trinidad-born British writer (1932–2018) known for novels and travel writing, awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2001.

kazuo-ishiguro.name: Kazuo Ishiguro
kazuo-ishiguro.summary: Japanese-British novelist awarded the 2017 Nobel Prize in Literature, best known for the Booker Prize-winning novel The Remains of the Day (1989).

four-quartets.name: Four Quartets
four-quartets.summary: A set of four poems by T. S. Eliot, published between 1936 and 1943, meditating on humanity's relationship with time and the divine.

ezra-pound.name: Ezra Pound
ezra-pound.summary: American poet and critic (1885-1972), a leading figure of early modernist poetry who shaped the work of Eliot, Joyce and Hemingway, and later collaborated with Fascist Italy in World War II.

invasion-literature.name: Invasion literature
invasion-literature.summary: A literary genre popular from 1871 to World War I about hypothetical foreign invasions of Britain, comprising over 400 novels and stories by 1914.

the-battle-of-dorking.name: The Battle of Dorking
the-battle-of-dorking.summary: An 1871 novella by George Chesney depicting a German-speaking power invading Britain, credited with starting the invasion-literature genre.

david-jones-painter.name: David Jones
david-jones-painter.summary: A British painter and modernist poet (1895–1974) whom Kenneth Clark in 1965 called the best living British painter, while T. S. Eliot and W. H. Auden ranked his poetry among the best of their century.

in-parenthesis.name: In Parenthesis
in-parenthesis.summary: 1937 work by David Jones based on his own experience as a First World War infantryman, mixing verse and prose and winning the Hawthornden Prize.

hugh-macdiarmid.name: Hugh MacDiarmid
hugh-macdiarmid.summary: Pen name of Scottish poet, journalist and political figure Christopher Murray Grieve (1892–1978), a leading force behind the Scottish Renaissance who wrote in a Scots literary language he developed himself.

mina-loy.name: Mina Loy
mina-loy.summary: A British artist, writer, poet and painter (1882–1966), one of the last first-generation modernists to achieve posthumous recognition, admired by T. S. Eliot, Ezra Pound and Gertrude Stein.

basil-bunting.name: Basil Bunting
basil-bunting.summary: An English modernist poet (1900–1985) best known for Briggflatts (1966), regarded as a major achievement of modernist poetry, and noted for his emphasis on reading poetry aloud.

paul-l-autaud.name: Paul Léautaud
paul-l-autaud.summary: French writer and theater critic (1872–1956) for Mercure de France, who signed his often caustic reviews with the pseudonym Maurice Boissard.

mavis-gallant.name: Mavis Gallant
mavis-gallant.summary: Canadian writer (1922–2014) who spent much of her life and career in France, best known as a short story writer but also a novelist, playwright and essayist.

jean-jacques-rousseau.name: Jean-Jacques Rousseau
jean-jacques-rousseau.summary: A Genevan philosopher and writer (1712–1778) whose political ideas, including in The Social Contract, shaped the Enlightenment and the French Revolution.

simon-armitage.name: Simon Armitage
simon-armitage.summary: English poet, playwright, musician and novelist born 1963, appointed Poet Laureate in 2019 and author of over 20 poetry collections.

kathleen-jamie.name: Kathleen Jamie
kathleen-jamie.summary: A Scottish poet and essayist born in 1962, who became Scotland's fourth Makar, or national poet, in 2021.

glyn-maxwell.name: Glyn Maxwell
glyn-maxwell.summary: British poet, playwright, novelist, librettist and lecturer, born in 1962.

bloodaxe-books.name: Bloodaxe Books
bloodaxe-books.summary: A British publishing house that specializes in poetry.

michael-moorcock.name: Michael Moorcock
michael-moorcock.summary: English writer, originally of science fiction and fantasy, also an editor and musician; best known for his Elric of Melniboné novels, hugely influential on 1960s–70s fantasy.

england-invaded.name: England Invaded
england-invaded.summary: Anthology of Victorian and Edwardian invasion-literature fiction edited by British author Michael Moorcock, first published in hardback in 1977 and reissued as a paperback in 1980.

romain-rolland.name: Romain Rolland
romain-rolland.summary: French dramatist, novelist and essayist awarded the Nobel Prize for Literature in 1915, admired for his idealism and known for correspondence with figures like Tagore and Freud.

honor-de-balzac.name: Honoré de Balzac
honor-de-balzac.summary: French novelist and playwright (1799 to 1850) regarded as a founder of realism in European literature, best known for the novel sequence La Comédie humaine.

mile-zola.name: Émile Zola
mile-zola.summary: French novelist and journalist (1840–1902), a leading figure of literary naturalism, best known for defending the wrongly convicted officer Alfred Dreyfus in his article J'Accuse...!

georges-feydeau.name: Georges Feydeau
georges-feydeau.summary: French playwright (1862-1921) of the Belle Époque, remembered for farces written between 1886 and 1914 such as La Dame de chez Maxim.

gcse.name: GCSE
gcse.summary: Academic qualification taken in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, introduced in 1986, covering subjects such as English, maths, science and history.

jean-cavaill-s.name: Jean Cavaillès
jean-cavaill-s.summary: A French philosopher and logician (1903–1944) specializing in philosophy of mathematics and science, who joined the French Resistance and was shot by the Gestapo in 1944.

dominion.name: Dominion
dominion.summary: A self-governing country within the British Empire and Commonwealth, mainly in the first half of the 20th century, including Australia, Canada, the Irish Free State, New Zealand, Newfoundland and South Africa.

french-section-of-the-workers-internatio.name: French Section of the Workers' International
french-section-of-the-workers-internatio.summary: A French social democratic party founded in 1905, uniting Marxist and reformist socialists, which led the 1936 Popular Front government under Léon Blum before becoming the Socialist Party in 1969.
french-section-of-the-workers-internatio.source_title: French Section of the Workers' International

socialist-party-france.name: Socialist Party
socialist-party-france.summary: A centre-left French political party founded in 1969, one of France's two dominant parties for decades, which first won power under Mitterrand in 1981.

renaissance-french-political-party.name: La République En Marche!
renaissance-french-political-party.summary: A French centrist political party founded by Emmanuel Macron in 2016 (now called Renaissance), which won an absolute majority in the 2017 legislative election.

national-rally.name: National Rally
national-rally.summary: French far-right political party, known as the National Front until 2018, founded in 1972 and led for decades by Jean-Marie Le Pen and then his daughter Marine Le Pen.

harold-wilson.name: Harold Wilson
harold-wilson.summary: Prime Minister of the United Kingdom from 1964–1970 and 1974–1976, and Labour Party leader from 1963–1976, the only Labour leader to win four general elections.

denis-healey.name: Denis Healey
denis-healey.summary: A British Labour politician (1917-2015) who served as Defence Secretary from 1964 to 1970 and Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1974 to 1979.

east-of-suez.name: East of Suez
east-of-suez.summary: A British political and military phrase for interests east of the Suez Canal, popularized by Rudyard Kipling's 1890 poem 'Mandalay'.

harold-macmillan.name: Harold Macmillan
harold-macmillan.summary: British Prime Minister and Conservative Party leader from 1957 to 1963, nicknamed "Supermac"; he succeeded Anthony Eden after Eden resigned following the Suez Crisis.

eoka.name: EOKA
eoka.summary: A Greek Cypriot nationalist guerrilla organization that fought British rule in Cyprus seeking union with Greece; its campaign ended in 1959 with independence granted the following year.

london-and-z-rich-agreements.name: London and Zürich Agreements
london-and-z-rich-agreements.summary: A 1959 set of agreements among Turkey, Greece, the UK and Cypriot leaders that led to Cyprus's independence in 1960.

akrotiri-and-dhekelia.name: Akrotiri and Dhekelia
akrotiri-and-dhekelia.summary: A British Overseas Territory of two areas on Cyprus with British military bases, retained by Britain under the 1960 treaty that granted Cyprus independence.

new-ecological-and-social-people-s-union.name: New Ecological and Social People's Union (NUPES)
new-ecological-and-social-people-s-union.summary: A 2022 left-wing French electoral alliance formed to deny President Macron a majority, which won the second-most seats but underperformed expectations.
new-ecological-and-social-people-s-union.source_title: New Ecological and Social People's Union

the-ecologists.name: The Ecologists
the-ecologists.summary: Centre-left to left-wing green political party in France, formed in 2010 from the merger of The Greens and Europe Ecology, and a member of the European Green Party.

rally-of-the-french-people.name: Rally of the French People
rally-of-the-french-people.summary: A right-wing French political party led by Charles de Gaulle, existing from 1947 to 1955.

union-of-democrats-for-the-republic.name: Union of Democrats for the Republic
union-of-democrats-for-the-republic.summary: A Gaullist political party in France from 1967 to 1976, successor to Charles de Gaulle's earlier movements, renamed several times before dissolving into the Rally for the Republic.
union-of-democrats-for-the-republic.source_title: Union of Democrats for the Republic

rally-for-the-republic.name: Rally for the Republic
rally-for-the-republic.summary: A Gaullist and conservative political party in France, founded by Jacques Chirac in 1976 as heir to earlier Gaullist movements; one of France's two major parties until it merged into another party in 2002.

union-for-a-popular-movement.name: Union for a Popular Movement
union-for-a-popular-movement.summary: Liberal-conservative French political party in the Gaullist tradition, one of France's two major parties until it was succeeded by The Republicans in 2015; its leader Nicolas Sarkozy became president in 2007.

the-myth-of-sisyphus.name: The Myth of Sisyphus
the-myth-of-sisyphus.summary: Albert Camus's 1942 philosophical essay introducing his philosophy of the absurd, concluding that one must imagine its central figure, Sisyphus, happy.

albert-camus.name: Albert Camus
albert-camus.summary: French philosopher, writer and political activist (1913–1960) who won the 1957 Nobel Prize in Literature and whose ideas helped shape absurdist philosophy.

sisyphus.name: Sisyphus
sisyphus.summary: In Greek mythology, the founder and king of Corinth condemned in the underworld to eternally push a boulder uphill after cheating death.

simone-weil.name: Simone Weil
simone-weil.summary: French philosopher, mystic, political activist and labourer (1909–1943) whose ideas on religion, spirituality and politics remain widely influential.

the-need-for-roots.name: The Need for Roots
the-need-for-roots.summary: A book by Simone Weil, published posthumously in 1949, diagnosing the spiritual and cultural malaise of 20th-century civilization and calling for renewed 'rootedness.'

g-e-moore.name: G. E. Moore
g-e-moore.summary: An English philosopher (1873–1958) who, with Bertrand Russell, helped found analytic philosophy and moved British thought away from idealism, advocating common-sense concepts in ethics, epistemology and metaphysics.

bertrand-russell.name: Bertrand Russell
bertrand-russell.summary: English philosopher, logician, mathematician and social reformer (1872-1970), regarded as a founder of analytic philosophy, who wrote over 70 books on mathematical, philosophical and political topics.

philosophical-society-of-england.name: Philosophical Society of England
philosophical-society-of-england.summary: British society founded in 1913 to promote philosophy among the general public, bringing together professional and non-professional philosophers; still publishes its journal, The Philosopher.

the-philosopher.name: The Philosopher
the-philosopher.summary: Long-running periodical established in 1923 by the Philosophical Society of England, originally in print and now existing in two competing formats since a mid-2010s split.

absurdism.name: Absurdism
absurdism.summary: Philosophical theory holding that the universe is irrational and meaningless, putting anyone who seeks meaning in conflict with a world that cannot provide it.

the-stranger-camus-novel.name: The Stranger
the-stranger-camus-novel.summary: 1942 novella by Albert Camus, his first published novel, following an indifferent man who kills an Arab man in French Algeria after his mother's funeral.

philippa-foot.name: Philippa Foot
philippa-foot.summary: English philosopher (1920–2010) who helped found contemporary virtue ethics and, with Judith Jarvis Thomson, is credited with inventing the trolley problem.

trolley-problem.name: Trolley problem
trolley-problem.summary: A thought experiment in moral philosophy about whether to sacrifice one person to save several others, raised by Philippa Foot in 1967 and later named by Judith Jarvis Thomson in 1976.

g-e-m-anscombe.name: G. E. M. Anscombe
g-e-m-anscombe.summary: A British analytic philosopher (1919–2001) and student of Wittgenstein whose 1958 article introduced the term 'consequentialism' into analytic philosophy and whose 1957 monograph Intention was called the most important work on action since Aristotle.

alasdair-macintyre.name: Alasdair MacIntyre
alasdair-macintyre.summary: Scottish-American philosopher (1929–2025) whose 1981 book After Virtue is among the most important 20th-century works of moral and political philosophy; taught at Notre Dame and other universities.

aristotle.name: Aristotle
aristotle.summary: Ancient Greek philosopher and polymath (384–322 BC) who founded the Peripatetic school, tutored Alexander the Great, and laid groundwork for modern science.

antony-flew.name: Antony Flew
antony-flew.summary: English philosopher (1923–2010) known for advocating atheism for most of his career before controversially declaring belief in an intelligent designer in 2004.

john-hick.name: John Hick
john-hick.summary: English philosopher and theologian known for his work on theodicy, eschatology and religious pluralism.

gaston-bachelard.name: Gaston Bachelard
gaston-bachelard.summary: French philosopher (1884–1962) who introduced the concepts of epistemological obstacle and epistemological break, influencing later French philosophers such as Michel Foucault.

epistemological-rupture.name: Epistemological break
epistemological-rupture.summary: A concept introduced in 1938 by French philosopher Gaston Bachelard, describing the moment scientific thought breaks away from an unconscious 'epistemological obstacle' blocking its progress.

metaxy.name: Metaxy
metaxy.summary: A concept from Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy meaning 'between,' describing humanity's place between opposing poles of existence, later developed by thinkers such as Eric Voegelin and Simone Weil.

pope-paul-vi.name: Pope Paul VI
pope-paul-vi.summary: Head of the Catholic Church from 1963 to 1978, who completed the Second Vatican Council's reforms and improved relations with Orthodox and Protestant churches.

ren-girard.name: René Girard
ren-girard.summary: A French academic (1923–2015) known for mimetic theory, which holds that imitative desire drives rivalry and violence and underlies the scapegoat mechanism in religion and culture.

georges-canguilhem.name: Georges Canguilhem
georges-canguilhem.summary: French philosopher and physician (1904-1995) who specialized in epistemology and the philosophy of science, particularly biology.

vitalism.name: Vitalism
vitalism.summary: The idea that living things are set apart from non-living matter by special vital forces beyond physics and chemistry; now regarded as a superseded or pseudoscientific theory.

modern-moral-philosophy.name: Modern Moral Philosophy
modern-moral-philosophy.summary: A 1958 essay by G. E. M. Anscombe that criticized consequentialism, coined that term, and influenced the later revival of virtue ethics through Alasdair MacIntyre.

after-virtue.name: After Virtue
after-virtue.summary: A 1981 book on moral philosophy by Alasdair MacIntyre, arguing modern moral discourse is irrational and praising Aristotle's ethics; a key text in the revival of virtue ethics.

georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.name: Hegel
georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.summary: German philosopher (1770–1831) and major figure in German idealism, whose dialectical system, 'absolute idealism,' shaped modern metaphysics, political philosophy and philosophy of religion.

alexandre-koj-ve.name: Alexandre Kojève
alexandre-koj-ve.summary: A Russian-born French philosopher (1902–1968) whose seminars on Hegel deeply influenced 20th-century French philosophy.

emmanuel-levinas.name: Emmanuel Levinas
emmanuel-levinas.summary: French philosopher of Lithuanian Jewish ancestry (1906–1995) known for his work in Jewish philosophy, existentialism and phenomenology, focused on the relation of ethics to metaphysics.

georges-bataille.name: Georges Bataille
georges-bataille.summary: French writer, essayist and theorist (1897-1962) whose work spanned literature, philosophy, anthropology and religious studies, exploring themes like sacrifice, eroticism and the sacred.

jean-paul-sartre.name: Jean-Paul Sartre
jean-paul-sartre.summary: A French philosopher and writer (1905–1980) and leading figure of existentialism, awarded the 1964 Nobel Prize in Literature, which he attempted to refuse.

graham-priest.name: Graham Priest
graham-priest.summary: British philosopher and logician born in 1948, distinguished professor at the CUNY Graduate Center and a visiting scholar at universities including Melbourne and St Andrews.

dialetheism.name: Dialetheism
dialetheism.summary: The philosophical view that some statements can be both true and false at once, challenging traditional logic and giving rise to contradiction-tolerant paraconsistent logics.

noneism.name: Noneism
noneism.summary: A theory in logic and metaphysics holding that some things do not exist, coined by Richard Routley in 1980 and revived by Graham Priest in 2005.

an-introduction-to-non-classical-logic.name: An Introduction to Non-Classical Logic
an-introduction-to-non-classical-logic.summary: A 2001 philosophy textbook by Graham Priest introducing non-classical propositional logics such as modal, intuitionistic, many-valued, relevant and fuzzy logic.

jules-vuillemin.name: Jules Vuillemin
jules-vuillemin.summary: French philosopher, 1920 to 2001, professor of philosophy of knowledge at the Collège de France who introduced analytical philosophy to France.

p-tanque.name: Pétanque
p-tanque.summary: A French boules sport in which players throw metal balls to land closest to a small target ball called the jack, codified in its current form around 1907–1910 in La Ciotat, Provence.

constitutional-council-france.name: Conseil constitutionnel
constitutional-council-france.summary: France's highest constitutional authority, established in 1958, which rules on whether proposed or enacted laws conform to the constitution.

welsh-church-act-1914.name: Welsh Church Act 1914
welsh-church-act-1914.summary: An Act of the UK Parliament that disestablished the Church of England in Wales and Monmouthshire, creating the separate Church in Wales, coming into force in 1920.

24-hours-of-le-mans.name: 24 Hours of Le Mans
24-hours-of-le-mans.summary: Endurance sports car race held annually near Le Mans, France, since 1923, won by whichever car covers the greatest distance in 24 hours.

stade-de-france.name: Stade de France
stade-de-france.summary: The national stadium of France, near Paris, built for the 1998 World Cup, whose final it hosted when France beat Brazil 3–0.

george-orwell.name: George Orwell
george-orwell.summary: Pen name of English writer Eric Arthur Blair (1903–1950), best known for Animal Farm and Nineteen Eighty-Four, whose work gave rise to the term "Orwellian."

a-nice-cup-of-tea.name: A Nice Cup of Tea
a-nice-cup-of-tea.summary: A 1946 essay by George Orwell laying out eleven rules for making the perfect cup of tea, including his firm view that milk should be added after the tea.

the-standard-london-newspaper.name: London Evening Standard
the-standard-london-newspaper.summary: London newspaper launched in 1827, known at various times as The Standard or Evening Standard, and for decades one of the city's main regional papers.

the-road-to-wigan-pier.name: The Road to Wigan Pier
the-road-to-wigan-pier.summary: 1937 book by George Orwell documenting bleak working-class living conditions in industrial northern England, followed by an essay on his own upbringing and views on socialism.

historic-england.name: Historic England
historic-england.summary: A British government body that protects England's historic environment by listing historic buildings, scheduling ancient monuments, and registering historic parks and gardens.

listed-building.name: Grade I
listed-building.summary: Part of the UK's listed building system protecting structures of special architectural or historic interest, restricting demolition, extension or alteration without permission.
